title: F1 to introduce full-time race stewards from 2027
text:
Formula 1's governing body the FIA is to introduce permanent race stewards from the 2027 season.

The move follows consistent calls from grand prix drivers for the change because of criticisms of inconsistency of decisions regarding penalties for on-track incidents.

The FIA said in a statement that it would begin recruiting permanent stewards, and was planning a "phased introduction" during the 2027 season.

The FIA statement added: "The introduction of dedicated full-time stewards to the FIA's flagship championship will provide continuity and expertise within the stewarding structure, further advancing the FIA's commitment to fairness through the ongoing review and continuous improvement of sporting regulations and stewarding guidelines.

"It will also allow for deeper implementation of best practice and greater consistency in decision-making."

It said that the use of driver stewards, usually an ex-F1 driver, would continue, "recognising the invaluable expertise they bring".

The plan is for "a small number" of full-time stewards to be recruited during 2027 and the group to be expanded from 2028.

"Existing FIA stewards will continue to play a vital role, contributing their experience within a mixed roster of full-time and part-time stewards for the foreseeable future," the statement said.

In reality, the move is not a major step on from the current situation, where a small number of stewards are rotated around races.

Each grand prix has a group of four stewards, one of which is an ex-driver.

Current drivers have often referenced the fact that they had repeatedly complained during briefings with FIA officials that rulings on driver standards and racing errors were not applied on a consistent basis.

Last year, Williams driver Carlos Sainz, a director of drivers' body the Grand Prix Drivers' Association, said: "F1 and the FIA all agree that [permanent stewards] should be the way forward, where at least two of the three stewards are permanent and we have one rotational for teaching purposes."

The decision follows the opening of an FIA race operations centre at F1's Biggin Hill headquarters in south London.

The FIA has in recent years received increased income from F1 - which provides the majority of its funding - on the basis that this would be applied to improving officialdom and rule-making.

FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem said: "This latest major investment in FIA officiating reflects our dedication to delivering the highest standards of decision-making, fairness and integrity in motorsport.

"The recruitment of full-time stewards is a significant step in our longstanding mission of building a dedicated officiating ecosystem in the FIA Formula 1 World Championship, it is also an investment in the future of our sport."

title: Verstappen 'trusts' F1 over Middle East decision
text:
Max Verstappen says he "trusts" Formula 1 has made the right decision in pressing ahead with the final two races of the season in the Middle East.

Last week, F1 stood down preparations for a substitute race at Imola in Italy if the events in Qatar and Abu Dhabi could not be held because of ongoing conflicts in the area.

The sport will now conclude the season in the Middle East, unless the situation deteriorates before the Qatar event on 27-29 November and Abu Dhabi on 4-6 December.

Verstappen said: "I trust F1 and FIA to make the right call on that, right?

"I don't have all the intel. I'm not an officer. I just hope that they make the right call on that. And that's all that you can rely on, really.

"They also send over their findings and understanding. So I trust them."

No trust problem with Ferrari team - Hamilton

How sporting events are being affected by Middle East conflict

Yamaha will not travel to Qatar for MotoGP race

Verstappen had previously voiced his opposition to ending the season in the Middle East.

"Normally I am happy to go to Qatar and Abu Dhabi, but you know, when there is a war nearby, and if some of the countries are in conflict with each other, then I think we shouldn't go," Verstappen said in September.

The Red Bull driver's fresh remarks reflect a uniform public stance in F1 on the situation, even though there are widespread misgivings among personnel about travelling to the Middle East in the context of the two conflicts in the area.

Last Sunday Iran targeted a US military base in Bahrain with a drone attack for the second time in three days, the latest salvo in the war launched against the country by the US and Israel in February.

And Houthi rebels in Yemen are advancing in their war against the Saudi-backed government of the country.

Missile attacks from the Houthis into Saudi Arabia are threatening that country's chances of hosting the second grand prix of next season, which is scheduled for 19-21 March.

McLaren's Lando Norris said that while he is "fine" with the decision to race, he is concerned about the "big team" behind him.

"I have my friend's wedding in Bahrain next week, so I was planning on going there and then going on to Qatar and then Abu Dhabi," he added.

"But it's not about me. It's a lot more people. It's the fans, it's the team personnel, so the question is for them, more than I would say it is for myself."

Mercedes driver George Russell said he has "no hesitation" in racing and that while he's "sure some people have their reservations" he doesn't "know of anyone who's concerned".

"I know people who live in the region and they said it quite bluntly, if they didn't feel comfortable they wouldn't be there with their families," he said.

"When you look around the world there are a lot of terrible things going on.

"You've just got to trust in the people. If they say it's safe, then you trust in them. F1 aren't stupid and I'm sure there's plans A, B, C, D, etc. So fingers crossed it'll all be fine."

MotoGP, which is owned by the same US group as F1, held a race in Qatar last weekend without problems.

F1, which has significant commercial links with the Middle East, has been closely monitoring the situation and has been advised by security officials and government figures in the Gulf and Europe that the races can go ahead, and there is no official advice against travelling to Qatar or Abu Dhabi.

F1 said in a statement last week that it was still prepared to cancel the two races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi if the situation deteriorated.

"If the situation develops negatively in the coming weeks before the events in the Middle East, we will not hesitate to do the right thing and the safety of everyone will always be the priority," an F1 spokesperson said on Tuesday.

title: No trust problem with Ferrari team - Hamilton
text:
Lewis Hamilton says there is "definitely not" a trust problem between him and his Ferrari team.

The seven-time champion has twice in the past four races ignored a call to pit for fresh tyres, both times to his competitive disadvantage.

The most recent time, in the Sao Paulo Grand Prix on 8 November, Hamilton stayed out on worn slick tyres in worsening rain and ended up spinning before pitting on the next lap.

Before this weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix, Hamilton spoke positively of his relationship with his race engineer Carlo Santi.

"We're constantly working on our communication," said Hamilton, who had a different race engineer last year.

"It's been a lot better this year. Carlos (sic) has done an amazing job. And those particular two times, particularly the last time, was just I didn't have the information I needed. I got the call right at the last minute.

"We'll just continue to work on the processes. We're super united in what's working, in the right direction."

The previous time Hamilton ignored a call to pit was in Singapore, when he decided to stay out during a virtual safety car period. He later apologised .

At the following race in Austin, he explained that he was "always looking at ways to win, always looking at doing potentially something different. And I wanted to be on a different strategy, not just the same strategy as Charles (Leclerc), where we just follow each other".

Ferrari's Hamilton-Leclerc problem - and other F1 stories to follow

'We've got big problems' - Hamilton says Ferrari need 'serious talks'

Verstappen 'trusts' F1 over Middle East decision

Hamilton and Leclerc both insisted that relations between the pair were good after clear-the-air talks in Brazil following a disagreement at the previous race in Mexico, where a tangle on the first lap led to them throwing away a potential one-two and handing victory to Red Bull's Max Verstappen.

Hamilton said in Las Vegas on Wednesday: "Charles is a great driver. The detail we went into about stuff like that in terms of when we close the visor, it's very clear we understand each other.

"We understand each other's boundaries and the ultimate goal, which is to get the best result for the team.

"So I don't feel that that will be a problem going forward. I have no concerns or worries about racing him, and I don't think he does with me either."

Leclerc said: "The discussion went very well. Very, very quickly, after a few sentences already, the tension that was there was not there anymore, and it was all fine.

"We both work in the direction of having that second place in the constructors' championship. The second place in the constructors' is important.

"It's also true that we've got a relatively big margin behind, which doesn't mean we need to minimise that, and we still have to work as a team. But what is really important for me now is to try and win before the end of the season and win the race."

He added that "everything has been taken out of proportion" but he is "kind of used to it" have been at Ferrari since 2019.

"Of course, the goal is not always to agree, and that will never happen," he added.

"We can have different opinions, and that was the case, for example, in Mexico. But just the fact of speaking eased all tensions, and we were completely fine with it.

"It's not that we had to speak for an hour, even though it ended up lasting an hour, just because we had a good time and we started speaking about also many other things in trying to bring the team and to help the team go forward.

"But the discussion about the tension was like maybe five or 10 minutes, and then the air was clean, and that's it."
